title: The Effects of School Spending on Educational and Economic Outcomes
research_question: Does an increase in per-pupil public K–12 school spending during childhood causally improve students' long-run educational attainment and adult economic outcomes (such as wages, family income, and the incidence of poverty)? Do any such effects differ by children's family income background, and through which school inputs do they operate?
data_description: The authors construct a panel of per-pupil school district spending in the United States covering 1967 and annually 1970–2010, drawn from the Census of Governments, the Historical Database on Individual Government Finances, and the CCD School District Finance Survey (F-33), with all dollars deflated to 2000 dollars. These data are linked, using 1969 school district boundaries, to restricted-use geocoded Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) records for individuals born 1955–1985 and followed through 2011. Outcomes include years of education, high school graduation, wages, adult family income, and adult poverty status, observed at ages 20–45. The analysis sample contains 93,022 person-year observations on 15,353 individuals from 1,409 school districts across 1,031 counties and all 50 states plus DC. Auxiliary data include 1960–1990 censuses, OCR data, county-level expenditure data on Head Start, AFDC, Medicaid, food stamps, Title I, and information on hospital and school desegregation timing.
institutional_context: Before the 1970s, most U.S. K–12 funding came from local property taxes, generating large within-state spending gaps between affluent and poor districts. Beginning with a 1971 court ruling and accelerating through the 1980s, state supreme courts in 28 states (1971–2010) overturned existing school finance systems on equity or, later, adequacy grounds, prompting legislatures to overhaul funding formulas. Reforms typically aimed to raise spending in low-spending districts and weaken the link between district wealth/income and educational resources. States adopted varying formula types—foundation plans, spending limits, reward-for-effort matching, equalization, and equity-based redistribution—producing heterogeneous spending changes across districts depending on each district's pre-reform spending and income level and the specific formula adopted. Cohorts born 1955–1985 straddle these reforms, so children in the same district experienced markedly different school-age per-pupil resources depending on birth year, state, and district characteristics.
